title: Ashtpadi 5, salok: giving and taking
hook: the salok warns against clinging to gifts and forgetting the Giver

segments.voice: Yesterday, ardaas: a room on its feet before the Ardas. Your line was to you, this prayer. Today, the fifth ashtpadi opens with a warning.

Hold your hand out, palm up, a coin resting on it. Now close your fist around it. Tighter. Your knuckles go white. Your whole arm is busy, and you can't pick anything else up, or wave, or shake a hand. Same coin, two ways of holding it. Ashtpadi five of Sukhmani Sahib is about those two hands, and it opens with a short couplet, a salok, about what happens when the fist forgets who put the coin there.
screen: `A COIN ON AN OPEN PALM.` → `THE SAME COIN IN A FIST.` → `TWO WAYS OF HOLDING.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. In the first, Guru Arjan names God denhaar, the Giver, literally the one whose nature is to give, and describes people who leave the Giver and attach themselves to other tastes, other pleasures. Not bad things, necessarily: things that were given, now held as if they made themselves. The second line, signed Nanak, says such people never truly succeed, and that without the Name their honor slips away. Notice what the salok doesn't say. It doesn't call the gifts wicked. The last ashtpadi named water, a breeze, family and hands among the gifts. The trouble starts when the gift crowds out the Giver. A few stanzas later, the ashtpadi gives a picture for it. Someone falls in love with the shade of a tree. But shade moves with the sun. It passes, and he's left with regret in his mind. The shade was real, and a gift. It just wasn't a possession. That line between giving and taking runs through this whole ashtpadi. What comes from the Giver is received. What's clung to as mine feels taken when it leaves. So the Sikh word here is not renouncing. Guru Arjan was a householder, and Sikhs are asked to live in the world. The word is holding: open palm, not fist.
screen: `DENHAAR: THE GIVER.` · `THE GIFT CROWDS OUT THE GIVER.` · `IN LOVE WITH A TREE'S SHADE.` · `OPEN PALM, NOT FIST.` · then, large: `HOLD GIFTS LOOSELY.`

segments.voice: Rest a small thing on your open palm, a phone, a ring, a key, and think where it came from. Close your hand tightly around it for three breaths and feel the effort, then open it again and let it simply rest there as you breathe, the way someone sits in the shade, glad of it, not needing to own it.
Denhaar, the Giver: ashtpadi five opens with a salok about the Giver, and the people who keep the gift and forget the One who gave it.
Your line: hold gifts loosely. Same coin, held in an open hand. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the start of the fifth ashtpadi; some readers take one ashtpadi a day, beginning with its salok.

fork.setup: you're resting in a tree's cool shade on a hot road. what do you do with it?
options: fence it off as your own.
enjoy it, glad, knowing it moves with the sun.
refuse to sit in it at all.
fork.reveal: in the ashtpadi, the one who loves the shade as if it would last ends in regret; the shade was a gift, not a possession.

original.note: Gurmukhi: denhaar, the Giver, the one whose nature is to give; the salok's name for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: the salok says having things is the problem.
what it means: the problem is the fist: keeping the gift and forgetting the Giver.
what a scholar hears: the -haar ending forms an agent noun (the one who gives); some commentators read the shade as maya, the passing world.
recall: a humble plea, with folded hands
guess: the Giver, the one whose nature is to give
a debtor who must repay what he took
a beggar who receives what others give

chat.says: Does Sukhmani say it's wrong to enjoy nice things?
options: No: gifts aren't wicked; trouble starts when the gift crowds out the Giver. Hold them openly.
Yes: it says Sikhs should give up comforts and leave home to live in the forest.
No: it says whatever you own is yours to grip, since you earned all of it yourself.
chat.meaning: The salok warns about leaving denhaar, the Giver, for the gifts; Guru Arjan was a householder, and the picture is an open palm, not a fist.
